questions.q: A query uses ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 50000 and a matching index exists. Roughly how many index entries does PostgreSQL read?
questions.explain: An index is sorted, but it has no "row number" to jump to. The database reads the rows in order and throws away the first 50,000. The cost of a page grows with its offset, which is why deep pages and full exports get slow.
options: 20, because the index lets it jump to row 50,000
About 50,020: it walks past every skipped row and discards it
50,000, because the 20 returned rows are already cached
All rows in the table, because OFFSET disables the index

questions.q: What does keyset (cursor) pagination send to the database to get the next page?
questions.explain: Keyset pagination describes the next page by values: "rows that sort after (created_at, id) of the last row I saw". With a matching index the database jumps straight to that point, so every page costs the same.
options: The page number, multiplied by the page size
The ids of every row already shown
The sort values of the last row shown, so the query can ask for rows after them
A server-side cursor that keeps a transaction open between requests

questions.q: In PostgreSQL, when is (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) true?
questions.explain: A row comparison is lexicographic, like sorting words: compare the first column, and only on a tie compare the next. That matches an index on (created_at, id), which is why PostgreSQL can use the index for it.
options: When created_at < $1 and id < $2 are both true
When either created_at < $1 or id < $2 is true
When created_at < $1, or when created_at = $1 and id < $2
Only when the two rows have the same created_at

questions.q: A cursor stores only the created_at of the last order, and the next page uses WHERE created_at < $1. Several orders share a timestamp. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: The remaining tied orders are not older than the last one, they are the same age, so < excludes them. Add a unique tie-breaker (the id) to the sort, the cursor and the comparison.
options: Nothing, as long as the sort is created_at DESC
Tied orders appear on two pages
Orders with the same timestamp as the last one shown, but not yet shown, are skipped
The query becomes slow because it cannot use the index

questions.q: Why should the last column in a paginated ORDER BY be unique, even with offset pagination?
questions.explain: Rows that compare equal may come back in any order, and that order can change between two runs of the same query. A unique tie-breaker gives every row exactly one position, so pages are repeatable.
options: Because PostgreSQL refuses ORDER BY on non-unique columns with LIMIT
Because SQL gives no fixed order among tied rows, so a tied row can move between pages from one request to the next
Because unique columns are always indexed
Because it makes COUNT(*) faster

questions.q: You paginate by (shipped_at, id), but shipped_at is NULL for unshipped orders. What happens to them with WHERE (shipped_at, id) < ($1, $2)?
questions.explain: A comparison with NULL is unknown, not true, so those rows drop out of every page after the first. Sort by NOT NULL columns, or use the same COALESCE(...) in the index and the query.
options: They sort first and appear on page 1
They appear on every page
After the first page, they never match the comparison, so they are never shown
PostgreSQL throws an error for NULL in a row comparison

questions.q: A client edits the cursor it received. Assuming your server decodes it, validates its types and passes its values as SQL parameters, what is the worst the edit can do?
questions.explain: With typed values passed as parameters and authorization taken from the session, a forged cursor only moves the starting point. That is why authorization must never live in the cursor.
options: Read orders that belong to another customer
Run arbitrary SQL
Start the page at a different position in the same result set the client may already see
Nothing at all: a cursor cannot be edited

questions.q: A teammate suggests putting customerId inside the cursor "so the next page knows whose orders to load". What is the problem?
questions.explain: Encoding is not protection. A cursor is client input. Authorization is decided on every request from the authenticated user, never from anything the client sends back.
options: It makes the cursor too long for a URL
Anyone can edit the cursor and read another customer's orders; who may see what must come from the verified session
Customer ids are not allowed in base64
There is no problem if the cursor is base64url encoded

questions.q: A client gets a cursor from ?status=paid and sends it with ?status=shipped. What is the best response?
questions.explain: A cursor belongs to one sort and one set of filters. Mixing them gives pages that make no sense. Binding the cursor to a fingerprint of the filters lets you answer with a clear client error.
options: Ignore the cursor and return the first page of shipped orders
Use the cursor anyway and return whatever matches
400, saying the cursor does not match these filters
500, because the request is inconsistent

questions.q: The order that a keyset cursor points at is deleted before the client asks for the next page. What happens?
questions.explain: A keyset cursor stores values, not a pointer to a row. "Rows with (created_at, id) less than these" is well defined even if no row has exactly those values anymore.
options: The server must return 404
The next page works normally: the query asks for rows after the stored values, whether or not that row still exists
The next page repeats the whole previous page
The next page is empty

questions.q: Why does listOrders ask the database for limit + 1 rows?
questions.explain: One extra row answers "is there more?" cheaply. The extra row is not sent; the cursor is built from the last row that is sent.
options: To make up for an off-by-one error in OFFSET
If the extra row exists there is a next page, so it can return a next cursor without counting all rows
So the client can see one row of the next page
Because LIMIT in PostgreSQL is exclusive

questions.q: A product manager wants "Showing 1-20 of N" on a 50-million-row orders list. Which answer is sound?
questions.explain: An exact count visits every matching row, the cost keyset pagination removed. Estimates (such as the planner's statistics) or an on-demand count keep normal paging fast.
options: Run SELECT count(*) on every page request; it is cached by PostgreSQL
Omit the exact total, or show a labelled estimate, or offer an exact count on a separate endpoint used only when needed
Compute the total by multiplying the page number by 20
Store the total in the cursor

questions.q: Which of these is a good fit for plain offset pagination?
questions.explain: Offsets are simple, allow jumping to page 7, and are fast enough on small tables that rarely change during paging. Feeds, syncs and exports need cursors.
options: An infinite-scroll activity feed with new items every second
A nightly job that copies all 30 million orders to accounting
An admin table of 2,000 suppliers with page numbers
A mobile app syncing a user's full order history

questions.q: Which test would catch the "order shown twice, another never" bug?
questions.explain: The bug only appears when data changes during paging and pages are compared as a whole. A test that reproduces those conditions fails for offsets and passes for correct cursors.
options: Fetch page 1 of a 10-row table and check it has 10 rows
Walk every page of a large table while inserting new rows between requests, and assert that each original row appears exactly once
Check that the response has a next_cursor field
Check that page 2 is different from page 1

questions.q: You add a currency field to every order in the response. When does this break a client?
questions.explain: Additive changes are safe for tolerant readers. Document that clients must ignore unknown fields, and write your own clients that way, and additions become free.
options: Never; adding is always safe
Always; any change needs a new version
When the client rejects fields it does not know, instead of ignoring them
Only when the client is written in TypeScript

questions.q: Which change is the most dangerous for existing clients?
questions.explain: Same name, different meaning: nothing crashes, every client just shows amounts 100 times too large. Change units only under a new name or a new version.
options: Adding an optional ?customer= filter
Adding a delivery_eta field
Keeping the field name total but sending kobo instead of naira
Adding a new endpoint /v1/refunds

questions.q: Is lowering the maximum limit from 100 to 50 a breaking change?
questions.explain: Tightening validation turns valid requests into errors. Keep the old rule for old versions, or ship the change in a new version.
options: No, because the server still returns valid pages
Yes: a request with limit=100 that worked yesterday now gets 400
Only if the database has fewer than 100 rows
No, clients must always send the default limit

questions.q: Your API chooses the version from a Shop-Version header, and a CDN caches GET responses. What must you add?
questions.explain: Caches key on the URL unless told otherwise. Vary lists the request headers that change the response, so a v2 body is never served to a v1 client.
options: Cache-Control: no-store on every response
Vary: Shop-Version, so the cache keeps separate copies per version
A version number in the response body only
Nothing; caches read all headers automatically

questions.q: A request sends Shop-Version: 2026-9-1, which is not a version you have. What should the server do?
questions.explain: Guessing puts the client on a version it was never tested against, silently. A clear 400 makes the typo visible at once.
options: Use the latest version
Use the oldest version
Answer 400 with a message naming the unknown version
Ignore the header and use the account's default without telling the client

questions.q: What is the main advantage of "one current implementation plus version changes" over copying the code for each version?
questions.explain: Copies drift: a fix applied to one copy is missing in the others. Version changes translate the single current response backwards, and the list of changes doubles as a changelog.
options: Old versions run faster
Logic and bug fixes exist once; each old version costs only small, documented translation functions
Clients no longer need to send a version
It removes the need for tests

questions.q: What do the Deprecation and Sunset response headers tell a client?
questions.explain: RFC 9745 defines Deprecation (a date, written as @ plus a Unix timestamp) and RFC 8594 defines Sunset (an HTTP date). A Link with rel="deprecation" points at the migration guide.
options: Deprecation: the server is overloaded; Sunset: retry after this time
Deprecation: since when this resource is deprecated; Sunset: when it will stop working
Both are cache headers for time-based expiry
Deprecation: the request used a wrong method; Sunset: the session expires

questions.q: After the sunset date, which status code should a retired version answer with?
questions.explain: 410 says "this existed and has been removed on purpose". A redirect to v2 would send old clients a response shape they cannot parse.
options: 404 Not Found
410 Gone, with a body that links to the migration guide
301 Moved Permanently to the new version
500 Internal Server Error

questions.q: A cursor keeps only the timestamp. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first page ends on order 5 with at = 2. "Less than 2" skips orders 4 and 3, which have the same timestamp. That is the tie bug; the fix is to compare (at, id).

questions.q: The same data, now compared on (at, id). What does this print?
questions.explain: The cursor is order 3 (at 2, id 3). Orders 2 and 1 have a smaller at, so they come next, and order 3 itself is excluded because its id is not smaller than 3.

questions.q: A new order arrives between two offset pages. What does this print?
questions.explain: The new order 6 goes to the front and pushes everything one place down. Offset 2 now starts at order 4, which was already shown. Deletes do the opposite and skip a row.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Sorting the names makes the fingerprint independent of the order the filters were written in. With no filters the key is the empty string, so the last line is empty.
options:
true
status=paid

false
status=paid

true
status=paid
undefined

true
status="paid"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON keeps the number a number. The padding = signs were removed when encoding, and atob accepts the unpadded text, so the round trip works.
options: 88412 number false
88412 string false
88412 number true
undefined undefined false

questions.q: A decoder checks the id in a cursor. What does this print?
questions.explain: A string is never a safe integer, even "88412". 2 ** 60 is too large to be exact. -3 is a safe integer, so a real decoder also checks the range (for example, at least 1) if negative ids are impossible.
options: [ true, false, false, false, true ]
[ true, true, false, false, false ]
[ true, false, false, true, true ]
[ true, false, false, false, false ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With four rows available, the fourth proves there is more. With exactly three, there is no extra row, so this is the last page. Returning hasMore: true there would make clients request an empty page.
options:
{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: true }
{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: false }

{ data: [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ], hasMore: true }
{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: false }

{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: true }
{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: true }

{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: false }
{ data: [ 1, 2, 3 ], hasMore: false }

questions.q: Which version changes apply to a client pinned to 2026-06-01?
questions.explain: Dates in YYYY-MM-DD form compare correctly as strings. A client on 2026-06-01 already has that change, so only the two later changes must be undone for it.

questions.q: Two version changes are undone in the wrong order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each undo expects the shape that existed right after its own change. Undoing the older change first finds no total_kobo yet, so undefined / 100 is NaN. Undo newest first.
options: { id: 1, total: 5000 } { id: 1, total: NaN, total_kobo: 500000 }
{ id: 1, total: 5000 } { id: 1, total: 5000 }
{ id: 1, total_kobo: 500000 } { id: 1, total: 5000 }
{ id: 1, total: 5000 } { id: 1, total: undefined, total_kobo: 500000 }

questions.q: What does this tolerant client print for a status it has never seen?
questions.explain: The unknown status falls back to a safe label, and the unknown eta field is simply not read. That is what makes additive server changes harmless.
options: [ 'Paid', 'Updated', 'On its way' ]
[ 'Paid', undefined, 'On its way' ]
[ 'Paid', 'refunded', 'On its way' ]
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Date.UTC counts months from 0, so 8 is September and 2 is March. The Deprecation header wants seconds, hence the division by 1000; Sunset uses the HTTP date format that toUTCString produces.

questions.q: Write nextPage(orders, after, limit). orders is sorted newest first by (at, id) descending. after is null or the last order of the previous page. Return the next limit orders. Walk all pages of size 2 and print each page's ids joined with commas.
questions.explain: Compare the timestamp first, and the id only on a tie, exactly like (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) in SQL. Comparing only at would lose orders 6, 4 and 3.

questions.q: Write encode(obj) and decode(token) for base64url cursors (no +, / or =). decode returns null for anything that is not valid. Print the round trip of { v: 1, k: [88412] }, whether the token contains =, and decode("%%%").
questions.explain: atob throws on characters that are not base64, and JSON.parse throws on text that is not JSON. Catching both and returning null lets the endpoint answer 400 instead of crashing.

questions.q: Write checkCursor(data, filters) for a decoded cursor object. Return "ok" when data.v === 1, data.f equals the filter key (names sorted, name=value joined by &), and data.k is [isoDateString, safeInteger]. Otherwise return "version", "filters" or "invalid", checked in that order.
questions.explain: Each check turns a different client mistake into a specific 400 message: an old cursor, a cursor reused with other filters, and damaged or forged values. The id must be a real integer, not the string "42".

questions.q: Complete render(order, clientVersion) so a client pinned to an older version gets the older shape. Undo only changes newer than the client's version, newest first. Print the order for 2026-01-15 and 2026-09-01 with JSON.stringify.
questions.explain: The newest change is undone first because each undo expects the shape right after its own change. A client on the newest version gets the current object untouched.

questions.q: Write resolveVersion(path, headers, fallback). The major version is the first path segment and must be v1 or v2 (else { status: 404 }). The dated version is the shop-version header or the fallback, and must be one of 2026-06-01, 2026-09-01 (else { status: 400 }). Otherwise return { major, dated }.
questions.explain: Resolving the version once at the edge, and rejecting unknown values, means no request is ever handled by a version it did not ask for. "latest" is refused on purpose: a client pinned to "latest" breaks every time you ship.

questions.q: Write breakingChanges(oldSample, newSample) that compares two response objects field by field and returns a list: "removed X" for a field that disappeared and "retyped X" for a field whose typeof changed. Added fields are not breaking. Print the result for the two samples in the starter.
questions.explain: Only the old sample's fields matter: they are what existing clients read. total_kobo and currency are additions and pass. The rename shows up as a removal, which is exactly how an old client experiences it. Contract tests in the API contracts lesson do this with full schemas.

questions.q: Orders are shown newest first. Write newerPage(orders, before, limit) that returns the limit orders just newer than before (compare (at, id)), still newest first. With the starter data, the page newer than order 3 with limit 2 must be [5, 4]. Print the ids.
questions.explain: The orders newer than 3 are 6, 5 and 4. The ones next to order 3 are the oldest of those, so read them in ascending order, take limit, and reverse back. Taking the first two of the newest-first list would give 6 and 5, skipping order 4.
